name: EVERY BREATH YOU TIKKA MASALA BURGER

recipe.history:
Tikka masala traces its roots to the Indian subcontinent, where the technique of marinating meat in spiced yogurt and cooking it in a tandoor oven — tikka — has existed for centuries. The word tikka itself derives from the Persian and Urdu word for 'bits' or 'pieces,' and the practice of coating those bits in aromatic spice pastes before high-heat cooking is deeply embedded in Mughal culinary tradition. The masala, meaning a spiced sauce or gravy, was a natural companion, transforming dry tikka into a rich, saucy dish. Long before any restaurant claimed the invention, cooks across the Punjab region and beyond were building complex tomato-cream sauces layered with cumin, coriander, garam masala, and fenugreek, serving them over tender charred chicken as both comfort food and celebratory feast.

The famous — and fiercely contested — Scottish-Indian debate concerns who first served chicken tikka masala as a cohesive restaurant dish in the Western world. One popular legend credits Ali Ahmed Aslam of the Shish Mahal restaurant in Glasgow, who allegedly improvised the dish in the 1970s by adding a can of tomato soup and cream to satisfy a customer who found his chicken too dry. Glasgow city councillors once petitioned for European Union protected status for the dish on these grounds. Indian culinary historians, however, push back firmly, arguing the dish is simply an adaptation of Punjabi murgh makhani — butter chicken — and that it was being served in Indian restaurants across Britain and beyond well before any Glasgow origin story solidifies. The debate remains unresolved, but both sides agree on one thing: once tikka masala existed in a bowl, it was impossible to stop eating it.

I remember the first time tikka masala stopped being a restaurant order and became something I made with my own hands. It was a rainy Tuesday, the kind where the windows fog up and the apartment smells like wet coats, and I had half a can of crushed tomatoes, a container of plain yogurt that needed to be used, and a stubborn optimism about the spice cabinet. I bloomed the cumin and coriander in butter until the kitchen filled with that deep, nutty smoke, then added the tomatoes and watched the sauce turn the color of a late October sunset. When I tasted it, something clicked — not just in the recipe, but in the understanding that a great sauce is a kind of patience made edible. The next logical step, naturally, was to put it on a burger, because a great sauce deserves to meet a great patty, and medium rare beef deserves to meet the world.

Medium rare is not a preference — it is a philosophy. Cooking a beef patty to an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit means respecting the fat, the fiber, and the flavor that the animal and the grind have to offer. At that temperature, the proteins have set just enough to hold the patty together while the center remains yielding, pink, and saturated with juice. The Maillard reaction has done its work on the crust, producing the bitter-sweet caramelized bark that contrasts with the cool interior. A well-seared medium rare patty does not bleed — it weeps, slowly, into the bun, seasoning everything it touches. To cook further is to squeeze out that juice, to tighten the fibers past forgiveness, to trade succulence for safety theater. The tikka masala sauce on this burger is bold and fragrant, and it demands an equally bold foundation — and only medium rare delivers that.
instructions: 1. Make the tikka masala sauce: Melt butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden, about 6–8 minutes.
2. Add the minced garlic and grated ginger to the pan and cook for 1 minute until fragrant, stirring constantly to avoid burning.
3. Add the tomato paste and stir to coat the onion mixture. Cook for 2 minutes, allowing the paste to caramelize slightly and deepen in color.
4. Add all dry spices — garam masala, cumin, coriander, smoked paprika, turmeric, cayenne, and salt — and stir vigorously for 30 seconds to bloom the spices in the fat.
5. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and stir to combine. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer uncovered for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and the raw tomato smell cooks off.

6. Stir in the heavy cream, yogurt, and sugar. Simmer for another 3–4 minutes until the sauce is glossy, richly orange, and coats the back of a spoon. Taste and adjust salt. Remove from heat and stir in fresh cilantro. Set aside.
7. Make the raita spread: Combine Greek yogurt, fresh mint, lemon juice, and a pinch of salt in a small bowl. Stir until uniform. Refrigerate until assembly.

8. Form the patty: Gently divide and shape the ground beef into a single patty approximately 4.5 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Create a shallow dimple in the center with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Do not overwork the meat.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy-bottomed pan over high heat until smoking. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat.
10. Place the patty in the pan and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to develop a deep, dark crust. Do not press the patty.

11. Flip once and cook for an additional 2–2.5 minutes. Begin checking internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer inserted horizontally into the center of the patty. Target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove the patty from heat at 130°F, as carryover cooking will bring it to the ideal range. Do not cook beyond 135°F.
12. Transfer the patty to a wire rack and rest for 3 minutes. Do not cover — trapping steam will soften the crust.
13. While the patty rests, toast the brioche bun: Melt 1 tbsp butter in the same skillet over medium heat and place the bun cut-side down. Toast for 60–90 seconds until golden brown.
14. Assemble the burger: Spread raita generously on the bottom bun. Layer on butter lettuce, cucumber slices, red onion rings, and the tomato slice.
15. Place the rested medium rare patty on top of the vegetables.
16. Spoon 2–3 generous tablespoons of warm tikka masala sauce directly over the patty, allowing it to pool and drape over the edges.
17. Garnish with fresh cilantro leaves. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately alongside remaining tikka masala sauce for dipping.
